title: Crochet and Knitting Starter Kits That Keep You Past the First Project
dek: Ten things for learning to crochet or knit, ranked by how much easier they make the first few projects. The yarn matters more than the gadgets.
seo_title: The hooks, needles and yarn that make learning to crochet or knit easier. Ten picks ranked by how much they help a beginner finish their first projects.
hero_image: balls of chunky yarn, crochet hooks and a half-finished scarf in a basket
intro: Crochet and knitting are relaxing, portable and cheap to start, which is why so many people try them. Many stop after a few frustrating evenings, usually because they started with the wrong yarn: dark, fuzzy or splitty, so they could not see their stitches. The right starting materials make the learning much faster.
This list is ordered by how much each item helps. Smooth, light-coloured yarn and ergonomic hooks or needles come first. Then the small accessories that make projects easier to finish.

Prices below are approximate street prices at the time of writing and move around constantly, especially during sale events. Treat them as a rough band for budgeting, not a quote. Always check the live listing before you buy.
how_we_pick: These picks come from craft teachers, fibre arts communities and long-run owner reports, cross-checked against current retail listings. We have not personally tested every item here. Free video tutorials and beginner patterns are widely available and are the best teacher alongside these supplies.

products.name: Smooth, light-coloured worsted weight yarn
products.tag: The thing that makes learning easier
products.image: skeins of light-coloured smooth acrylic yarn
products.body: Beginners need to see each stitch clearly. Smooth, light-coloured worsted weight yarn shows stitches well and does not split. Avoid dark colours, fluffy mohair, chunky chenille and velvet yarns until you are confident; they hide stitches and are hard to undo. Acrylic or cotton blends are cheap and forgiving. Buy extra, because practice uses a lot. The case for it: easy to see stitches, cheap for practice, and forgiving. The trade-off is real: acrylic is less warm than wool and novelty yarns are hard for beginners, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used.
cons: Acrylic is less warm than wool
Novelty yarns are hard for beginners

products.name: Ergonomic crochet hooks
products.image: a set of crochet hooks with soft rubber handles
products.body: Thin metal hooks cause hand cramps in long sessions. Hooks with soft, thick handles are much more comfortable, especially for people with arthritis. A set covering 2-6mm handles most yarns; a 5mm hook suits worsted weight. Clover Amour and similar sets are popular. The case for it: less hand strain, covers most yarn weights, and good for long sessions. The trade-off is real: cheap sets have rough hooks that snag and check sizes are marked, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. For $10-25, it is a small, low-risk addition to the list rather than a centrepiece purchase you need to think hard about.
cons: Cheap sets have rough hooks that snag

products.name: Bamboo or wooden knitting needles
products.image: bamboo knitting needles with a small swatch
products.body: Metal needles are slippery, and stitches slide off, which frustrates beginners. Bamboo and wood have a bit of grip, which keeps stitches on the needle. Start with a medium size such as US 8 (5mm) for worsted weight yarn. The case for it: stitches stay on, warm and light, and quiet. The trade-off is real: thin wooden needles can snap and slower than metal once experienced, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $10-20, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use.

products.name: Stitch markers
products.body: Stitch markers mark the start of a round, pattern repeats or increases. For crochet, they are almost essential for amigurumi and working in rounds. Locking markers work for both crafts. The case for it: keeps your place, essential for rounds, and cheap. The trade-off is real: easy to lose and cheap plastic ones snag yarn, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $5-10, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way. As with anything on this list, check the exact listing details and current price before adding it to a cart.

products.name: A tapestry needle set
products.body: Finishing a project means weaving yarn ends in and sewing pieces together. Blunt tapestry needles with large eyes slide through stitches without splitting yarn. Bent-tip needles are easier. They are cheap and easy to lose, so buy a set with a case. The case for it: neat finishing, doesn't split yarn, and cheap. The trade-off is real: easily lost and plastic ones bend, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. For $5-8, it is a small, low-risk addition to the list rather than a centrepiece purchase you need to think hard about.

products.name: Small sharp scissors
products.body: Small, sharp scissors cut yarn cleanly and fit in a project bag. Embroidery scissors are the classic choice. Keep them only for yarn so they stay sharp. The case for it: clean cuts, portable, and cheap. The trade-off is real: pointed tips need a cover and dull quickly on paper, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $8-15, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use. None of that makes it essential for everyone reading this, only worth knowing about if the description above matches how you actually use the space.

products.name: A tape measure
products.image: a retractable tape measure beside a knitted swatch
products.body: Patterns give sizes and gauge, and checking your stitches per inch is how a sweater ends up fitting. A small retractable tape measure lives in the project bag. The case for it: check gauge and size, tiny, and cheap. The trade-off is real: cheap ones stretch and check it measures in both inches and cm, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $3-6, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way. As with anything on this list, check the exact listing details and current price before adding it to a cart.
cons: Check it measures in both inches and cm

products.name: A row counter
products.image: a click row counter on a table
products.body: Losing count of rows is one of the most common beginner frustrations. A click counter or ring counter keeps track. Phone apps work too, but a physical counter is quicker. The case for it: never lose count, cheap, and quick. The trade-off is real: must remember to click and apps work too, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. For $5-10, it is a small, low-risk addition to the list rather than a centrepiece purchase you need to think hard about. It is a minor purchase in the context of the whole set-up, but the kind that is easy to regret skipping once you notice the gap.

products.name: A project bag
products.image: a drawstring project bag with yarn and hooks
products.body: A project bag keeps yarn clean, stops tangles and makes it easy to take crafting on trips and commutes. Look for a yarn guide hole and inside pockets. The case for it: keeps projects together, portable, and protects yarn. The trade-off is real: nice-to-have, not essential and velcro snags yarn, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $10-25, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use. None of that makes it essential for everyone reading this, only worth knowing about if the description above matches how you actually use the space.

products.name: Interchangeable circular needle set
products.image: an interchangeable circular knitting needle set in a case
products.body: Once you are hooked on knitting, an interchangeable set with needle tips and cables in many sizes replaces dozens of separate needles and works for hats, sweaters and blankets. It is a big purchase, so buy it once you know you are sticking with it. The case for it: replaces dozens of needles, works for most projects, and lasts for years. The trade-off is real: connections can loosen and expensive for beginners, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $50-120, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way.

faq.q: Is crochet or knitting easier to learn?
faq.a: Many find crochet easier to start because there is only one live loop. Both are learnable in a weekend with video tutorials.

faq.q: What is a good first project?
faq.a: A dishcloth or a simple scarf. Small, flat and forgiving.
Some are, but many have poor hooks and yarn. Buying a few good pieces separately often works better.
